title: Throughput sanity runs & KV cache sleuthing (notes)
content:
Purpose

Quick working log for the throughput sanity sweep and focused KV-cache investigation started after the 2025-11-03 nightly regression alert (p95 tail widening on hosted-api routes). This doc captures commands, microbench configs, sample traces, initial hypotheses, and reproducible steps for follow-up. Treat this as a lab notebook: rough, iterative, lots of TODOs.

Context and symptoms

- On 2025-11-03 we saw a sustained ~12% drop in tokens/sec for standard text-generation workload on the 4xA100 pool during the 18:00-20:00 PST window. p50 unaffected; p95/p99 widened.
- Alert triggered by perf-regression-detector: trace delta spikes correlated with increased KV-cache miss rates in the metrics dashboard.
- Suspected intersection between scheduling prioritization, KV cache eviction policy, and kernel selection fallback causing occasional long tails.

Goals for this run

1) Reproduce the p95 spike locally with a minimal harness. 2) Verify if KV cache churn is necessary/sufficient for the tail. 3) Isolate whether scheduler preemption or kernel fallback is the source. 4) Produce an actionable mitigation (config tweak or hotfix PR).

Environment & versions

- runtime: serving-runtime@main @ commit 3c8b7f2 (branch: perf/kvprobe)
- gpu: AWS p4d.24xlarge equivalent in lab cluster (4 x A100-80GB)
- kernel lib: kernels-v2.1.4
- allocator: shared-allocator rev 1.9.0
- harness: probe-runner v0.3.7

Microbench harness config (sanity sweep)

- tool: probe-runner --mode=trace-seed --concurrency=32 --qps=120
- workload: prompt-length-distribution = {short: 60%, medium: 30%, long: 10%} (seq lens 8/128/1024)
- batching: continuous-batch=true, max_batch_size=32, latency_slo_ms=200
- kv settings toggled per run: {cache_enabled=true/false, ttl_ms=0/10000/60000, shard_count=16/64}
- scheduler policy: round_robin | latency_aware | throughput_first (sweep)
- sample window: 10k requests per config, with trace sampling rate 1/500 (to keep trace volume manageable)

Experiment matrix (high level)

- A: baseline (cache=true, ttl=60s, scheduler=latency_aware)
- B: cache off (cache=false, scheduler=latency_aware)
- C: cache=true, ttl=10s, scheduler=latency_aware
- D: cache=true, ttl=60s, scheduler=throughput_first
- E: cache=true, ttl=0 (no TTL but LRU eviction), scheduler=latency_aware

Quick results summary

- A (baseline): nominal throughput, p95 ~ 180ms. trace samples show occasional 500-800ms outliers (1 in 2000).
- B (cache off): p50 ~ same, p95 increased slightly in steady state but no extreme tails like baseline. Interesting: miss-rate increased but tails reduced.
- C (ttl=10s): transient higher miss-rate but p95/p99 unstable; tails more frequent than A.
- D (throughput_first): best steady throughput but worst p99 tail. Traces show long kernel stalls while a large batch is scheduled.
- E (ttl=0 LRU): increased eviction churn; p95 worse than A, many traces show repeated KV repopulation loops.

Interpretation notes

- Surprising finding: turning cache off removes the extreme tail events seen with cache on. That indicates the cache implementation/path can introduce latency worse than a cold-path for some sequences. Two candidate mechanisms: (1) lock contention or allocator-induced stalls during cache lookup/eviction, (2) cache-priming that triggers expensive kernel variants (larger memory working set) causing preemption or kernel fallback.
- Scheduler interacts: throughput_first batches aggressively and amplifies the tail by waiting longer for larger batches; small probability events (cache eviction) then get multiplied. Latency_aware is better but still occasionally hits long stalls — likely from internal allocator locks.

Representative trace excerpt (simplified timeline)

- request_id: rq-20251107-3a7
  - t=0ms: receive request, route to worker-17
  - t=2ms: kv-lookup start (shard-12)
  - t=2.5ms: kv-lookup blocked on allocator lock (owner: worker-9)
  - t=40ms: kv-lookup resume, returns miss
  - t=41ms: model kernel select -> fallback to fallback-kernel-quantized (incurs memcpy and unaligned dims)
  - t=120ms: kernel enqueue -> long wait in device queue (preempted by large batch job)
  - t=540ms: kernel complete, response sent

Root-cause hypotheses (ranked)

1) Shared allocator lock contention inside KV cache path causing multi-ms stalls; when combined with kernel fallback this produces long tail. Evidence: traces repeatedly show 'blocked on allocator lock' before long kernels.
2) Cache repopulation triggers different kernel variant selection (e.g., ONNX -> quantized fallback) that has worse device scheduling characteristics.
3) Scheduler batching policy magnifies rare cache stalls by clumping them into heavy device queues; throughput_first makes this worse.

Quick reproduction recipe (dev box)

1) git checkout perf/kvprobe ; bazel build //cmd/probe-runner
2) ./bazel-bin/cmd/probe-runner --mode=trace-seed --concurrency=32 --qps=120 --batching=max32 --cache-ttl-ms=60000 --kv-shards=16 --sample-rate=1/200
3) Run for 30 minutes; collect perf traces and device queue lengths (nvidia-smi dmon + runtime device queue depth exporter).

Investigation actions taken

- Added micro-instrumentation around allocator (hotpatch) to log lock hold times. Initial sample: median lock hold ~40us, 99.9th ~8ms during churn windows.
- Hypothesis test: replaced shared-allocator with per-shard arenas (local branch) -> immediate removal of 99.9th lock hold spikes in local runs, and p99 dropped ~35% in the limited run.
- Kernel-fallback audit: added logging to kernel selector to dump feature flags for any fallback case. Found 12 instances where fallback occurred due to unexpected sequence padding to 1024 dims after KV repopulation.

Open questions / things to validate

- Are allocator contention spikes coming from unrelated jobs on the same node (co-tenancy)? We saw some correlation with background maintenance tasks on a small subset of runs. Need to run in fully isolated nodes.
- What's the unit cost tradeoff for per-shard arenas (memory overhead vs latency tail improvement)? Run long-duration soak to confirm memory behavior.
- Is kernel fallback avoidable by selecting a more stable quantized variant, or by normalizing sequence lengths before kernel selection? Investigate fast-path heuristics in kernel selector.

Immediate mitigations proposed

- Short-term: adjust scheduler to prefer latency_aware for routes with high cache-usage; reduce max_batch_wait_ms default from 20ms to 8ms for tiered routes. (Config change - low risk)
- Mid-term: land per-shard allocator branch behind a feature flag and run canary on dedicated pool. (Code + rollout)
- Long-term: refine kernel selection to avoid fallback away from optimized kernels when a request is cache-repopulating; revisit kernel variant heuristics.

Action items (owners)

- Priya: run isolated node soak with per-shard allocator and memory profiler (target: 48h) — due 2025-11-24
- Logan: produce a short A/B config change to reduce max_batch_wait_ms for high-cache routes and observe p95 over 24h — due 2025-11-21
- Mariana: audit kernel selector logs and produce a list of sequence-length padding cases that triggered fallback — due 2025-11-19
- Ethan (me): prepare feature-flagged PR for per-shard arenas, include microbench harness and perf tests — PR draft by 2025-11-22

Notes to self / rough todo

- Add flamegraph capture step to probe-runner when trace delta > 50ms.
- Add a synthetic microbench where many small keys are continuously evicted to stress the allocator (tool: kv-evict-stress).
- Update alerting rule to include kv-cache miss rate as a correlation metric so future incidents point to this path.

Appendix: commands used (copyable)

- probe-runner example:
  ./bazel-bin/cmd/probe-runner \n    --mode=trace-seed \n    --concurrency=32 \n    --qps=120 \n    --batching=continuous \n    --max-batch-size=32 \n    --cache-ttl-ms=60000 \n    --kv-shards=16 \n    --sample-rate=1/200 \n    --log-level=debug

- quick allocator lock sampler (local):
  sudo perf record -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30; sudo perf script | flamegraph.pl > flame.svg

Endnotes

This doc is intentionally informal. Main takeaway: KV cache is not purely benign — under certain churn patterns it can amplify a tail via allocator contention and kernel-fallback interactions. Short-term config changes reduce exposure; per-shard arenas look promising for a code fix.

If you diverge from the steps above, please append a short note to this doc with results so we keep the lab notebook up to date.
